chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbaat, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali Al-Jurjani, from the one who narrated it, from one of the two (peace be upon them), who said:
Do not obligate upon yourself the rights (of others), and be patient with calamities, and do not enter into something whose harm upon you is greater than its benefit for your brother.
ai.seo_question: What are the key ethical principles regarding social obligations and patience in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In the Shia tradition, this narration from al-Kafi underscores the principle of *muraqaba* (self-monitoring) in social ethics, warning against *ghulw* (excess) in obligations that may lead to burnout or neglect of broader duties. It highlights the pragmatic wisdom of evaluating the net benefit (*manfa'a*) of commitments, ensuring that one's capacity for kindness to others remains sustainable amidst life's tribulations (*nawa'ib*).

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from sahl Bin Ziyad, from Ali Bin Asbaat, from Al Hassan Bin Ali Al Jurjany, from the one who narrated it, 
(It has been narrated) from one of the two (5<sup>th</sup> or 6<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>) having said:
‘You must not obligate upon yourself the right, and observe patience upon the calamities, and do not enter into something the harm of which upon you is greater than its benefit is for your brother’.
en.sarwar: 3. A number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ali ibn Asbat from al-Hassan ibn Ali al-Jurjaniy from those who have narrated to him ms who has said the following: “One of the two Imam, (abu Ja’far or abu ‘Abd Allah), ‘Alayhim al-Salam, has said, ‘

You must not obligate your soul for others’ rights; you must exercise patience in difficulties; and you must not involve yourself in an affair where its harm to you is greater than its benefit for your brother (in belief).”
